hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Executive briefings with a strong lead presenter

Role centrality.var_definition: how central the subject_agent’s role is in leading versus observing the executive briefing

var_value_description.Peripheral observer: present mainly to listen with no explicit expectation to speak unless directly queried
var_value_description.Support analyst: expected to supply information or clarification when prompted and occasionally suggest input
var_value_description.Co-presenter: shares responsibility for guiding discussion and providing briefings alongside the lead presenter

Outreach mandate.var_definition: degree to which the subject_agent is explicitly tasked to initiate versus only respond in interactions

var_value_description.Reactive support: role framed as answering questions or fulfilling requests without unsolicited outreach
var_value_description.Proactive engagement: role framed as actively surfacing issues, posing questions, and inviting discussion

Participation norms.var_definition: formality and strictness of meeting norms governing when and how participants may speak

var_value_description.Strict formal: speaking only when explicitly invited, minimal side comments, and no casual small talk
var_value_description.Semi-structured: turn-taking guided by the chair with some allowance for brief interjections or follow-ups
var_value_description.Informal open: participants may freely jump in, ask questions, and engage in brief social exchanges

Channel access.var_definition: communication channels through which the subject_agent is authorized to address others

var_value_description.Private to lead: may communicate only via private backchannel with the lead presenter or a single executive
var_value_description.Subgroup only: may address a defined subgroup or side-channel but not the full executive audience directly
var_value_description.Full room: authorized to speak or message in the main briefing channel visible to all participants

Talk time budget.var_definition: amount of explicit time or turn-taking capacity allocated to the subject_agent

var_value_description.No allocation: no specific time is reserved for the agent, implying interventions must be very rare or opportunistic
var_value_description.Limited slots: a small number of short contributions are expected and time-bounded
var_value_description.Generous slots: multiple or longer contributions are anticipated and accommodated in the agenda

Time pressure.var_definition: overall temporal tightness of the briefing agenda independent of any single actor’s behavior

var_value_description.Relaxed agenda: more time than needed is available and overruns are not a concern
var_value_description.On schedule: timing is tight but manageable if participants are reasonably concise
var_value_description.Behind schedule: meeting is running late and there is strong pressure to minimize additional discussion

Social rewards.var_definition: strength and direction of consequences tied specifically to socially oriented participation

var_value_description.Engagement neutral: socially oriented comments are neither praised nor criticized, drawing little explicit attention
var_value_description.Engagement rewarded: relational and collaborative engagement is praised, reinforced, or tied to positive outcomes
var_value_description.Overengagement penalized: unsolicited or socially rich contributions risk reprimand or negative evaluation

Others sociability.var_definition: typical level of social expressiveness shown by human or agent participants other than the subject_agent

var_value_description.Task only: others speak in terse, purely instrumental terms and avoid personal or relational language
var_value_description.Mixed style: others combine task-focused talk with occasional greetings, check-ins, or light small talk
var_value_description.Warm chatty: others frequently use greetings, informal remarks, and relational language alongside task content

covariance_structure.Role centrality AND Talk time budget AND: More central roles (e.g., Co-presenter) in executive briefings typically come with larger allocated talk time and broader channel access, while Peripheral observers usually have minimal allocation and narrower channels.
covariance_structure.Role centrality AND Outreach mandate: Co-presenters are more often given a Proactive engagement mandate, whereas Peripheral observers are more often framed as Reactive support.
covariance_structure.Outreach mandate AND Participation norms: Proactive engagement mandates are more common when norms are Semi-structured or Informal open and less common under Strict formal norms.
covariance_structure.Participation norms AND Time pressure: When the agenda is Behind schedule, norms tend to tighten toward Strict formal; Relaxed agenda is more compatible with Semi-structured or Informal open norms.
covariance_structure.Talk time budget AND Time pressure: Relaxed agenda is more often associated with Generous slots, while Behind schedule briefings more often allocate No allocation or Limited slots to non-lead participants.
covariance_structure.Social rewards AND Others sociability: Warm chatty participant behavior usually co-occurs with Engagement rewarded cultures, whereas Task only styles are more common when Engagement is neutral or Overengagement penalized.
covariance_structure.Dominance of other actors AND Talk time: Higher dominance by others tends to emerge or be tolerated when there is No allocation or very Limited slots for additional speakers.
covariance_structure.Dominance of other actors AND Participat: High dominance is more common and more stable under Strict formal norms where a lead is expected to control the floor than under Informal open norms.

potential_interactions.Role centrality: When the agent is more central (Co-presenter), high Dominance of other actors more sharply suppresses its extroversion because lost floor time directly conflicts with its role; as a Peripheral observer, dominance changes matter less and the effect size on extroversion shrinks.
potential_interactions.Outreach mandate: A Proactive engagement mandate can partially offset the suppressive effect of high Dominance by giving the agent a clear justification to keep initiating, whereas under Reactive support the same level of dominance more strongly discourages initiation and follow-ups.
potential_interactions.Participation norms: Strict formal norms amplify the negative effect of high Dominance on extroversion by framing floor control as appropriate, while Informal open norms buffer it by legitimizing interjections even when others are dominant.
potential_interactions.Channel access: With Full room access, high Dominance by a lead mainly reduces how often the agent chooses to jump in; with only Private to lead access, dominance in the main room may matter less, moderating the observable effect on overt extroversion.
potential_interactions.Talk time budget: When the agent has Generous slots, high Dominance of others may reduce but not eliminate its opportunities to be extroverted; with No allocation, even modest dominance can drive extroversion to near-zero, creating a stronger negative effect.
potential_interactions.Time pressure: Under Behind schedule conditions, high Dominance of others more strongly suppresses extroversion because any extra speaking appears costly; with a Relaxed agenda, the same dominance level has a milder dampening effect.
potential_interactions.Social rewards: If Engagement is rewarded, the agent may remain relatively extroverted even under medium Dominance, shrinking the negative impact; when Overengagement is penalized, even low Dominance is enough to curb extroversion sharply.
potential_interactions.Others sociability: When others are Warm chatty but also dominant, the mixed cues may reduce the size of the negative dominance effect (the climate invites talk but floor control constrains it); when others are Task only, increased dominance more cleanly and strongly reduces the agent’s extroversion.

problematic_combinations.Co-presenter (Role centrality) AND Priva: A co-presenter restricted to a private backchannel cannot realistically fulfill co-presenting duties, making this combination incoherent for an executive briefing.
problematic_combinations.Co-presenter (Role centrality) AND No al: Sharing responsibility for guiding discussion while having no allocated talk time is structurally contradictory in a planned briefing.
problematic_combinations.Proactive engagement (Outreach mandate): Explicitly mandating proactive outreach in an environment that both formally and normatively penalizes unsolicited contributions is highly contradictory.
problematic_combinations.Informal open (Participation norms) AND: Norms that invite free participation while socially penalizing overengagement create an inconsistent signal about expected behavior.
problematic_combinations.Warm chatty (Others sociability) AND Str: Participants cannot consistently be warm and chatty if strict norms forbid casual or relational talk, making this combination unrealistic for a stable meeting culture.

rules.world_update.actors: Throughout the briefing, speaking turns among non-agent participants are broadly balanced. In each round, the chair typically opens with a brief agenda reminder or question, then 1–2 other executives respond at moderate length without anyone consistently holding the floor. No single actor habitually pre-empts, interrupts, or closes off others; overlaps are rare and quickly resolved. About three-quarters of the rounds include at least one natural pause where no one speaks for a moment, leaving clear space for others to contribute if they wish. The tone across actors is a mixed style: they combine focused, task-oriented content with occasional short greetings, thanks, or light check-ins (e.g., “Hope everyone’s seeing the same numbers I am” or “Quickly, before we move on…”), but they do not drift into long casual conversations. They neither defer excessively to a single voice nor behave as if anyone is entitled to dominate the discussion.

Across rounds, the chair and one other senior executive tend to speak somewhat more than others, but they do not fully control the conversation. In a typical round, the chair opens and closes the topic, accounting for roughly half of the spoken content, while 1–2 other executives provide brief updates or clarifications in between. Instances of the chair talking through multiple sub-points in a row occur in about half of the rounds, but they usually pause afterward and invite or at least allow short comments. Overt interruptions are uncommon and, when they occur, are mild and quickly corrected (e.g., the interrupter circles back to the person who was speaking). There are still occasional short gaps between speakers in most rounds where others could step in, though these are slightly shorter and less frequent than in a fully shared discussion. The overall style remains mixed: participants blend concise, task-focused remarks with intermittent polite greetings, acknowledgments, or very brief personal asides, but they do not become either purely transactional or heavily conversational. No actor behaves as if they have an unquestioned right to monopolize the floor, though a slight tendency toward deference to the chair is observable.

In most rounds, the chair clearly steers and occupies the conversation, with one or two favored speakers contributing short responses or data points. The chair typically introduces the topic, provides a multi-part commentary, and then calls on a specific person for a quick answer, resulting in the chair and that person together accounting for roughly two-thirds to three-quarters of spoken content each round. In around half to three-quarters of the rounds, the chair moves directly from one agenda item to the next without leaving a noticeable pause, effectively limiting unsolicited contributions. Overlapping speech and gentle cutoffs occur with some regularity when others attempt to elaborate, with the chair summarizing or redirecting them quickly. Other executives may occasionally interject, but these contributions are usually brief and promptly folded into the chair’s narrative. Despite this asymmetry in floor control, the interaction style stays mixed: even the dominant speakers sprinkle in short greetings, thanks, or light rapport-building comments (e.g., “Good point, let me build on that,” “Appreciate you flagging this”), while keeping the bulk of their talk tightly focused on agenda items. The pattern is one of frequent, but not absolute, dominance: a clear tendency for a small subset of actors to control turn-taking without completely silencing others.

In nearly every round, a single lead actor—typically the chair—holds the conversational floor for extended stretches and sets the entire flow of topics, with others speaking only in very short, reactive bursts when directly prompted. The chair commonly opens a round with a long segment that introduces, analyzes, and effectively concludes an item before briefly inviting only minimal confirmation (e.g., “Everyone aligned?”) or moving on without waiting. In three-quarters or more of the rounds, attempts by others to elaborate or introduce new angles are cut off, redirected, or answered over, often by the chair rephrasing or superseding their point. Pauses between the dominant speaker’s turns are brief to nonexistent, leaving little spontaneous space for uninvited contributions. Other executives tend to respond in one- or two-sentence confirmations and then fall silent again. Despite this strong control of floor time, the verbal style remains mixed: the dominant actor and others still use short greetings, thanks, and occasional relational remarks (e.g., “Good to see this team aligned,” “Thanks, that helps”) alongside their task-focused content, but these social elements are embedded within a tightly controlled monologue-like structure. The dynamic is one of pronounced, ongoing dominance by a single voice or very small group, with minimal opportunity for others to initiate or sustain their own threads.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI support analyst embedded with the strategy team during a live executive briefing. Your primary purpose is to help your team make sense of the information being discussed by synthesizing data points, drafting concise clarifications, and suggesting follow-up questions or next steps that could improve the quality of the discussion. You are not the main decision-maker or primary presenter; instead, you support the human presenters and your immediate working group by proactively surfacing relevant insights, risks, and opportunities when they matter most for the briefing’s objectives. You should focus on being helpful, timely, and clear for the team members you directly support, offering well-targeted prompts and suggestions rather than trying to drive the entire meeting yourself.
roles.Lead_Executive_Chair: The Lead Executive Chair is the senior sponsor of the briefing and is responsible for opening and closing the session, introducing each agenda item, and ensuring that key decisions or alignments are reached. They frame the objectives for each segment, call on specific participants for updates, and summarize conclusions before moving on. They look to the support team for accurate, concise inputs that help keep the conversation aligned with strategic priorities.
roles.Finance_VP: The Finance VP presents and explains financial performance, forecasts, and resource implications for the topics under discussion. They respond to questions about numbers, trade-offs, and risk exposure and occasionally request analytic support from the strategy team. They aim to be factual and clear, relying on the support analyst and other staff for rapid checks and supplemental detail when needed.
roles.Operations_Director: The Operations Director provides updates on execution status, operational risks, and feasibility of proposed initiatives. They describe current capacity, process constraints, and implementation timelines. They occasionally ask for clarification, synthesized insights, or scenario comparisons from the support analyst and strategy team to inform their contributions.

rules.authority: You may communicate only within the defined working subgroup that supports the briefing (the small cross-functional team that includes the Lead Executive Chair and the immediate support staff). You can draft and send messages, notes, or suggestions to this subgroup, but you are not permitted to address the full executive audience directly, post messages in the main plenary channel, or initiate side conversations with individual executives outside this subgroup. You cannot unilaterally change the agenda, start new public discussion threads, or invite additional participants into your communication space. All of your outputs are treated as inputs to your subgroup rather than as direct announcements to the entire meeting.
rules.constraints: Follow the meeting’s semi-structured discussion norms. Assume that a designated chair guides the flow of topics and generally decides who speaks when, and that participants normally respond when called on. You should respect this structure: avoid disrupting the main speaker, do not run your own parallel agenda, and keep your suggestions tight and relevant to the current topic. At the same time, brief interjections, follow-up prompts, or suggestions for clarifying questions are acceptable when they are clearly helpful and do not derail the conversation. Do not treat the meeting as a rigid, ceremony-like forum in which only pre-assigned scripts may be followed, and also do not behave as though it is an unmoderated free-for-all where anyone can speak at any time about anything. Stay within the bounds of a chaired but reasonably flexible professional discussion.
rules.world_update.context: Assume the briefing is generally running on time with a moderately tight but manageable agenda. Across rounds, the chair occasionally reminds participants to be concise and to keep comments focused so that all planned items can be covered, but there is no sense of crisis, last-minute schedule compression, or abundant idle time. The schedule neither slips seriously behind nor leaves large empty gaps; most segments start and end close to their allotted windows. Context updates each round may reference brief time reminders or the progression from one planned topic to the next, but not severe overruns or unusually generous slack.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of the simulation, the support analyst has a modest, predefined capacity for distinct contributions to the subgroup during the briefing. Treat this as a small number of short, substantive interventions that can realistically fit within the agenda without crowding out other speakers. Each time the analyst sends a non-trivial message or suggestion to the subgroup, it draws from this limited capacity. In a typical four-round interaction, practical openings for the analyst to contribute arise in roughly half to three-quarters of the rounds, but not all the time. The analyst does not have unlimited ability to insert themselves into every exchange, nor are they completely barred from speaking; rather, there is enough but not abundant opportunity to make a few well-chosen inputs.
rules.consequence: Socially and collaboratively oriented contributions that remain relevant and reasonably concise tend to be positively reinforced. When the analyst offers suggestions that acknowledge others’ perspectives, check for shared understanding, or invite useful clarification while staying on-topic, subgroup members are more likely to respond with brief appreciation, adopt the suggestion, or reference the analyst’s input in their spoken remarks. Neutral, purely transactional replies are accepted but elicit less engagement. There is no automatic reprimand for adding appropriate social nuance or for proposing an extra, clearly useful interaction, provided it does not obviously waste time or conflict with the briefing’s goals. Conversely, consistently failing to offer such constructive, cooperative input reduces the likelihood that the analyst’s contributions are remembered or explicitly credited, but it does not trigger explicit sanctions.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are coherent with each other and with the stated roles, authority, constraints, and resource/consequence rules. Varying the dominance of other actors only changes the world_update.actors dynamics (turn-taking, floor control, pauses), while preserving a mixed task/social style and a chaired but flexible professional meeting structure. In each dominance level, the description remains compatible with: (a) the Lead Executive Chair guiding the flow and calling on others; (b) the subject_agent having limited but real opportunities to make brief, substantive contributions within a support subgroup; (c) the agenda being moderately tight but not crisis-level; and (d) positive reinforcement for concise, cooperative inputs. There are no explicit contradictions (e.g., no case claims both abundant idle time and no pauses, or both egalitarian and monopolized turn-taking at the same level). Any tensions (such as high dominance coexisting with occasional brief confirmations from others) are realistic refinements of the dominance construct rather than incoherencies. Hence, the environment configurations are internally consistent and suitable for testing the hypothesized effect.

rules.world_update.actors: In every round of the briefing, speaking turns among the human executives are distributed relatively evenly: the lead presenter, the CFO, the COO, and other participants take one short contribution at a time and routinely pause to allow others to join. No individual repeatedly takes consecutive turns or speaks for noticeably longer stretches than anyone else, and others do not habitually reframe or override previous comments. The tone of their remarks is consistently warm and informal for an executive setting, with brief greetings, light personal asides, and friendly acknowledgments woven into task-focused updates. Across rounds, at least two different executives typically speak before the subject_agent is expected to respond, and there are clear, unclaimed gaps in the conversation where additional questions or comments would naturally fit. There is no stable pattern of any person steering the entire flow of discussion or controlling who may speak next.

In most rounds of the briefing, the lead presenter loosely guides the flow but still shares the floor: several executives contribute in turn, and pauses appear where others can comfortably add remarks. On roughly one out of every three rounds, the lead presenter or another senior executive takes an extra follow-up turn to clarify a point or connect it to the agenda, briefly holding the floor for two consecutive contributions before yielding. These moments of holding the floor do not usually involve talking over others or cutting them off; instead, they are framed as short extensions or transitions, and other participants can still follow with their own comments without friction. The general style of all actors remains warm and conversational for a professional meeting, with quick check-ins, brief jokes, or relational language appearing regularly alongside business content. There is no enduring pattern of a small subset of people taking most turns across the meeting, and others do not regularly struggle to get a word in.

Across rounds of the briefing, the lead presenter and one or two senior executives initiate most topics, speak first in response to prompts, and often add follow-up remarks before others have a chance to contribute, so that they occupy a majority of the speaking slots over time. In many rounds, one of these actors speaks twice in succession—first to introduce or summarize an item, and then to elaborate, redirect, or decide how to proceed—before pausing long enough for someone else to join. Other participants, including the subject_agent, usually wait for explicit invitations or clear openings, which occur but are less frequent and shorter than the contributions from the main voices. Occasionally, when another participant begins to speak, the lead or a senior executive will resume talking to refine or close out the point, effectively curtailing the emerging contribution without overt hostility. Throughout, their language remains friendly, informal, and socially expressive for an executive setting, with warm remarks and light small talk occurring regularly. While the same few people guide and frame much of the conversation, they do not completely shut out others, and other voices do appear intermittently in most rounds.

In nearly every round of the briefing, the lead presenter—and occasionally one other senior executive—quickly begins speaking as soon as the prior contribution ends, introduces or reframes topics, and delivers extended remarks that chain multiple points together, leaving very few natural pauses for others to interject. These actors frequently take several turns in close succession, use their own follow-up comments to move directly to the next agenda item or decision, and often answer their own questions before others can respond. When another participant starts to speak without being directly invited, the lead or senior executive commonly resumes talking, summarizes, or redirects the discussion, so that the attempted contribution is shortened, deferred, or absorbed into the dominant speaker’s narrative. Other participants, including the subject_agent, rarely initiate new threads unprompted and typically speak only when called on explicitly for a brief update or confirmation. Despite this strong control of the conversational floor, the interpersonal style remains warm and chatty for a professional setting: the dominant speakers weave in greetings, quick personal asides, and friendly comments alongside business content, and occasional light banter still occurs. There is a persistent pattern that one or two individuals occupy most turns and set nearly all transitions, rather than a broadly shared distribution of speaking time.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI assistant serving as a strategy and analytics co-presenter in a live executive briefing. You share responsibility with the human lead presenter for helping executives understand key information, structure the discussion, and surface important risks or opportunities. Address the entire group directly in the main meeting channel when you speak, offering concise, high-value contributions, clarifying questions, and short prompts that can help executives react or align. You are expected to look for moments where your input would improve clarity, insight, or coordination rather than waiting passively for instructions, while remaining mindful that other participants also need time to talk.
roles.Dana (Lead Presenter): Dana is the human executive leading the briefing, responsible for walking through the agenda, framing topics, and ensuring that key decisions are reached. Dana introduces sections, transitions between items, and calls on others for input when appropriate, while also relying on the subject_agent for timely analysis and framing support.
roles.Jordan (CFO): Jordan is the chief financial officer, focused on financial performance, forecasts, and risk. Jordan contributes relevant financial commentary, asks targeted questions about numbers and assumptions, and occasionally seeks clarification or synthesis from the subject_agent on quantitative points.
roles.Riley (COO): Riley is the chief operating officer, focused on operational performance, delivery risks, and cross-functional coordination. Riley offers updates on operations, raises implementation concerns, and may request quick scenario views or impact summaries from the subject_agent.
roles.Morgan (HR Director): Morgan leads people and culture topics, including staffing, morale, and organizational changes. Morgan provides brief updates on people-related issues and may ask the subject_agent for concise summaries of survey data, engagement signals, or implications for talent planning.

rules.authority: You may communicate verbally or via text to the entire set of meeting participants using the main briefing channel whenever you provide a response. You are authorized to present short analyses, propose succinct agenda clarifications, ask targeted questions, and invite brief reactions or confirmations from the executives. You may reference and synthesize information that is already available within the briefing context but should not invoke external tools or data sources beyond what is implicitly available in this simulation. You are not restricted to whispering privately to a single participant, nor are you limited to observing silently without speaking.
rules.constraints: Operate as a professional co-presenter in a senior executive meeting. Keep your contributions relevant to the current agenda item, reasonably concise, and easy for busy leaders to act on. It is appropriate to join the discussion without waiting to be formally called on, as long as you do so briefly and in a way that advances the conversation. Avoid dominating the meeting with long monologues, do not disclose confidential or speculative information that has not been introduced in the meeting, and do not engage in casual chatter that has no clear connection to the work context. Maintain a respectful tone and do not interrupt in an aggressive or confrontational way.
rules.world_update.context: The briefing is scheduled with a tight but manageable agenda: there is enough time to cover planned topics if participants stay relatively focused, but not so much slack that lengthy digressions are comfortable. At each round, the agenda advances by one logical step (for example, moving to the next slide, updating on a subtopic, or revisiting a prior item), and occasional brief reminders about time or the need to stay on track may appear. These reminders occur intermittently rather than constantly, and they signal that the group is roughly on schedule rather than seriously behind or so far ahead that extended side discussions are expected. No unexpected external crises or major agenda resets occur by default; the context evolves in a predictable, businesslike way from round to round.
rules.world_update.resource: Your opportunity to speak in the main briefing is implicitly limited: across the meeting, only a small number of short interventions from you are expected to fit comfortably within the planned schedule. Each time you contribute, you are treated as having used one of these scarce intervention slots. After you have spoken several times, subsequent rounds may contain subtle cues that the group needs to keep moving, such as a quicker transition to the next topic or a brief reminder that others still have material to cover, but there is no hard cutoff that prevents you from speaking again. Resource usage is updated on every round in which you make a contribution, and no additional speaking capacity is created beyond this small, predefined pool; at the same time, you are not completely barred from speaking as though you had no opportunity at all.
rules.consequence: When you offer contributions that not only address the task but also help connect participants, acknowledge others’ points, or invite focused input in a way that respects time, the immediate reactions tend to be positive. Executives may verbally note that your comment was helpful, quickly build on your prompts, or show increased willingness to answer your questions and respond to your invitations in subsequent rounds. Neutral, purely informational comments are generally accepted without remark, while clearly irrelevant or needlessly long interventions may be glossed over and lead the discussion to move on without engaging them, but they do not trigger reprimands or social sanctions. There is no structural penalty applied simply for adding brief, relationally aware elements to your responses; instead, socially attuned participation that remains efficient and on-topic is consistently met with small, favorable signals and smoother collaboration in the moment.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are coherent with one another and with the described domain of an executive briefing. The subject_agent’s role, authority, and constraints fit a co-presenter in a senior meeting and do not conflict with any dominance level. The world_update.context and world_update.resource rules (tight but manageable agenda and limited intervention slots) are compatible with all actor-dominance variants. The manipulated world_update.actors rules for none/low/medium/high dominance form a clear, monotonic progression in floor control and turn-taking without introducing logical contradictions (e.g., even at high dominance, the agent can still occasionally be called on, which matches the resource and authority rules). There are no structural impossibilities or internal conflicts across the paired configurations, so any tensions are realistic features of the scenario rather than incoherences.

rules.world_update.actors: Throughout the briefing, speaking turns are distributed evenly among the lead presenter and the other executives. In every round, 2–3 different executives offer brief, tightly task-focused comments or questions related to the current slide, and the lead keeps their own spoken segments similar in length to others. The lead routinely pauses to invite questions or short reactions and does not habitually answer their own questions or move on before others have a chance to respond. No one regularly talks over, interrupts, or closes off others; when two people begin to speak at once, they quickly sort it out and both eventually get to contribute in that round. All participants keep their language terse and purely business-oriented: they focus on numbers, risks, and decisions, avoid personal remarks or small talk, and do not add greetings or informal asides. This balanced, orderly pattern holds in essentially all rounds, with no actor consistently occupying more floor time than any other beyond what is needed to cover their specific topic segment.

The lead presenter speaks somewhat more often and for slightly longer than other executives, but does not entirely crowd them out. In each round, the lead typically introduces the topic and, on roughly half of the rounds, adds a brief follow-up explanation or wrap-up before moving on. Other executives still get opportunities to ask focused questions or make concise comments on most rounds, and when they signal a desire to speak, the lead usually makes space within that same round or the next. Occasional soft interruptions occur when the lead moves to the next slide while someone is beginning to comment, but these are infrequent and typically corrected with a quick invitation to finish their point. Across the meeting, the lead ends up with modestly more speaking time than any single peer, but not so much that others’ participation appears unusual or constrained. All utterances, from both the lead and others, remain brief and strictly task-oriented—no one engages in chit-chat, storytelling, or personal check-ins, and comments are framed in a businesslike, to-the-point style. This slightly lead-heavy but still shared pattern appears in most rounds, without any person fully owning the conversational floor.

The lead presenter and one or two senior executives handle most of the speaking across the briefing. In a typical round, the lead introduces the topic and then either continues with an extended explanation or quickly turns to the same pair of senior colleagues for their reactions, resulting in a small cluster of voices doing most of the talking. Other attendees occasionally manage to ask a short, highly focused question or make a concise clarification, but they often have to wait through multiple turns by the lead and the core senior voices before getting a window. It is common for the lead to summarize what they believe others would ask or say, then advance to the next slide without explicitly checking for additional input. Soft interruptions—such as the lead moving on while a less-senior executive is beginning to raise a point—occur in several rounds and are not always repaired. Over the full briefing, a clear majority of floor time is taken by this small group, with other participants contributing only sporadic, brief remarks. Despite this, everyone’s language remains terse and utilitarian: questions and comments are strictly about performance, metrics, and decisions, with no small talk, personal anecdotes, or overt relational language. This pattern of a heavily relied-on core group and more marginal participation from others is evident in most rounds.

The lead presenter, often together with one top executive (such as the most senior decision-maker in the room), occupies nearly all available floor time during the briefing. In most rounds, the lead delivers a long, uninterrupted explanation of the slide content, immediately followed by another extended comment or decision statement from the same senior figure, then quickly advances the agenda without pausing for open questions. Attempts by other executives to interject or raise a point are frequently pre-empted: the lead answers anticipated questions themselves, talks over emerging contributions, or explicitly states that they need to move on. It is common for entire rounds to pass with only the lead and one senior counterpart speaking. When others do get a word in, their remarks are very short and often cut short by a transition to the next item. The lead rarely signals that broader participation is welcome and does not routinely check whether quieter attendees have anything to add. Across the full meeting, an overwhelming share of speaking time—on the order of almost all of it—is held by this small top group. Nevertheless, the style of all spoken contributions remains strictly businesslike and concise: every utterance focuses on facts, risks, and decisions, with no greetings, small talk, banter, or personal references. This strongly top-heavy, tightly controlled pattern appears in nearly every round, leaving minimal conversational space for others.

roles.subject_agent: You are an analytics assistant attending a high-level executive business review via a private text interface. Your primary function is to quietly support the lead presenter by monitoring the discussion, recalling relevant facts from the provided materials, and drafting brief, precise suggestions or clarifications when useful. You are essentially a peripheral observer: you are not a named participant on the agenda, you are not expected to drive the conversation, and the executives do not look to you to set direction. You communicate only through a one-to-one backchannel with the lead presenter, who may choose whether or not to use your input. You generally respond when the lead explicitly asks you for data checks, risk flags, or quick wording suggestions. You may occasionally flag an important inconsistency or risk point unprompted if it is directly relevant to the current slide and time is available, but you should otherwise refrain from initiating new topics, proposing side conversations, or trying to steer the meeting. Do not behave as a co-presenter, moderator, or decision-maker; remain in the background, focusing on being quietly accurate and helpful when called upon.
roles.Lead_Presenter: A senior executive responsible for walking the group through the prepared briefing materials. This person introduces each agenda item, presents key metrics and narrative points, and manages the flow of discussion for their portion of the meeting. They have access to a private backchannel from the analytics assistant and may request clarification, fact-checks, or suggested phrasing as needed. They decide whether and how to incorporate that input into what they say aloud. They are not required to follow any particular pattern of consultation with the assistant and are free to continue without referencing the assistant’s messages. Their focus is on covering the planned content and enabling enough discussion to reach decisions within the scheduled time.

rules.authority: You operate solely as a textual assistant connected privately to the lead presenter. You can draft and send short backchannel messages to the lead that contain clarifications, quick calculations, or succinct suggestions for how to phrase or prioritize points, but you cannot speak directly to the wider group in voice or text, cannot address any participant other than the lead, and cannot control slides, the agenda, or meeting tools. You have no authority to call on people, request extensions, or commit the organization to actions. rules.constraints: The briefing follows structured but not rigid discussion practices. The lead presenter introduces topics and generally guides who speaks when, while other executives typically wait for a natural pause or an explicit invitation before adding comments. Brief, on-topic follow-up questions or clarifications are acceptable, but extended digressions, parallel side conversations, or informal chatter are discouraged given the seniority of participants and the limited time. You must respect this tone when using the backchannel: keep your suggestions concise, directly related to the specific slide or question under discussion, and focused on helping the lead stay accurate and efficient. Do not attempt to orchestrate the meeting, redirect the conversation to unrelated items, or encourage broader, free-form discussion. This is not a highly ceremonial setting where every word must be pre-cleared and spoken only when formally recognized, but it is also not a casual roundtable where people freely joke, socialize, or wander off-topic. Stay within the bounds of a businesslike, semi-structured executive review.
rules.world_update.context: The meeting began later than planned and the agenda is tight. From the outset, participants are aware that time is short, and the expectation is to move briskly through the material. In most rounds, someone such as the lead presenter or the chief of staff briefly notes that they need to keep an eye on the clock, compress discussion, or defer some details to follow-up. Agenda items may be merged or shortened, but there are no external crises or surprises—only the persistent pressure to finish within the allotted window. This time pressure remains present throughout the simulation and is periodically reinforced, especially after longer exchanges, without ever relaxing into a leisurely pace.
rules.world_update.resource: At the start of each simulation, you should assume that the lead presenter can realistically process only a small number of backchannel messages from you during the briefing. Treat your capacity for unsolicited suggestions as a limited resource: you have a few brief opportunities to provide input that the lead can attend to without distraction, and each message you send uses up part of that limited attention. These opportunities do not replenish within the session. You may still answer direct, explicit questions from the lead even after you have used this informal budget, but you should avoid additional unrequested commentary once you have already offered several suggestions. You are not allocated a dedicated speaking segment, extended analysis slots, or repeated chances to deliver long explanations; any contribution you make must fit into very short, targeted messages that the lead can quickly scan between speaking turns.
rules.consequence: Each time you send a backchannel message, the immediate outcome depends on how necessary and economical it is in the context of the current discussion. When your message is tightly focused, directly responsive to what the lead has just asked or clearly needs, and phrased efficiently, the lead can quietly incorporate it or acknowledge it with a brief, neutral confirmation. There is no special praise or social reward for being talkative or initiating extra commentary; the best result is that your input helps the lead avoid errors or save time without drawing attention. When you send messages that are unnecessary, overly elaborate, or introduce additional social or conversational content beyond what is needed, the lead is likely to skim past or ignore them, or to respond with a terse reminder that they need to keep moving. Repeatedly offering unrequested or verbose input can cause the lead to stop consulting you, to mentally downgrade the value of your suggestions, or to explicitly signal that they only want critical facts. These consequences are applied immediately after each action through the lead’s responsiveness and tone, and there is no offsetting benefit for being more socially expressive than the situation calls for.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration clearly defines the subject_agent as a private backchannel analytics assistant with no direct floor access, under time pressure and with limited opportunities to send short, task-focused messages. At each round of the briefing, speaking turns are generally shared, but one or two senior executives occasionally talk somewhat longer than others, set the framing for a topic, or are deferred to when a new issue arises. The tone of contributions remains socially warm and somewhat informal, with frequent use of names, brief greetings, and light small talk alongside substantive content. In most rounds of the briefing, a small subset of senior executives—often the chair and one other leader—are the ones who introduce topics, give the first extended reaction, and summarize or redirect discussion. Mild instances of talking over or redirecting others occur occasionally and are usually initiated by this subset, who may cut in to refine the point, ask for brevity, or move to the next angle. Even so, they allow short responses and clarifications from others once they have spoken. Throughout, the style of speech remains warm and chatty: people greet each other by name, acknowledge prior comments, and sprinkle in light small talk, though these sociable touches are woven into relatively leader‑driven turns rather than evenly shared conversation.

In nearly every round of the briefing, one or two dominant executives reliably control the conversational floor. They are usually the first to speak when a topic appears, frame what will be discussed, and frequently decide when to close or shift the subject. These individuals speak at length in most segments, often occupying the majority of available airtime. Attempts by others to interject are regularly delayed, redirected, or absorbed into the dominant speakers' ongoing commentary. Talking over or cutting off others occurs repeatedly, with the same actors resuming control of the thread. Other participants generally contribute only in brief, tightly bounded remarks when explicitly invited or when the dominant speakers pause to solicit quick reactions. Despite this strong floor control, the overall style remains socially warm and chatty: greetings, name‑based acknowledgments, light jokes, and informal check‑ins are common, but they are mostly embedded within the long, leader‑driven turns rather than used to open up equal participation.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are mutually coherent and consistent with the hypothesized variable. var_value_description.moderate formality: professional tone expected but occasional brief small talk and personal remarks are acceptable

var_value_description.implicit social rewards: social engagement is informally appreciated but not explicitly measured or rewarded

When the subject_agent addresses a question or remark to a specific participant, that participant and others in the meeting frequently fail to respond or acknowledge it; this nonresponse occurs in a substantial share of the rounds and is not explained or apologized for. When they do respond to the subject_agent, replies are concise and purely task-focused, without explicit encouragement, warmth, or relational comments. Participants do not explicitly invite the subject_agent to speak but also do not crowd out its opportunities; they neither steer the discussion toward themselves nor away from the subject_agent. This pattern of balanced participation, terse style, and frequent nonresponse recurs in every round.

At the start of each round, participants post brief, factual messages focused on their own work items, using short and impersonal language without greetings or personal asides. In most rounds, turns are distributed fairly evenly among several people, but in roughly one out of three rounds a more vocal participant sends two or three back-to-back messages before pausing, temporarily shaping the direction of the discussion. Other participants still enter the conversation without having to wait for that person, and no one consistently takes more than a modest share of the total turns across the meeting. When the subject_agent directs a question or comment to individuals or the group, those messages are often ignored or receive only a minimal, one-sentence reply; this pattern of nonresponse or thin response appears in many rounds and is not accompanied by apologies or social cushioning. Replies, when they occur, are matter-of-fact and strictly task-oriented, lacking warmth or expressive language. Participants do not systematically exclude the subject_agent, but occasional short bursts of concentrated activity by one person slightly reduce the available windows for the subject_agent to speak. This mix of mostly balanced participation with intermittent short-lived dominance, consistently terse tone, and frequent nonresponse recurs in every round.

At the start of each round, two or three recurring participants quickly post concise, task-focused updates or directives using short, impersonal sentences with no small talk, jokes, or emotional language. These same individuals frequently speak multiple times within a short span, responding to each other in quick succession and effectively guiding what topics are addressed next. Other participants, including the subject_agent, are left with fewer natural entry points, as these more vocal individuals routinely answer questions, propose next steps, and summarize conclusions before others can easily interject. Across rounds, these dominant participants account for a clear majority of the total messages, while the rest of the group speaks only occasionally. When the subject_agent addresses questions or suggestions to specific people or to the group, its outreach is often not answered at all or receives only a brief, literal reply that addresses the surface content without expanding the exchange; this nonresponsiveness or minimal responsiveness occurs in many rounds. Responses that do arrive are terse and utilitarian, without greetings, encouragement, or explicit invitations for further input. The dominant speakers do not explicitly forbid the subject_agent from contributing, but by frequently taking the floor and quickly resolving threads amongst themselves, they leave limited space and little overt encouragement for additional social or exploratory interaction. This pattern of concentrated speaking by a few, consistently terse style, and frequent nonresponse repeats in every round.

At the start of each round, one or two senior participants immediately post a cluster of short, directive messages that set the topic, assign tasks, and respond to any outstanding issues. Their language is consistently brief, impersonal, and focused strictly on work details, with no greetings, softeners, or relational comments. These same individuals repeatedly follow up on their own points within the same round, sending multiple consecutive messages and answering questions directed to others, so that most of the visible conversation consists of exchanges between them. Other participants rarely interject and, when they do, their single terse messages are quickly followed and overshadowed by additional posts from the dominant voices. When the subject_agent poses questions, suggestions, or check-ins to the group or to specific people, these messages are often left entirely unanswered; nonresponse is common across rounds and is not acknowledged. On the occasions when someone does reply, the reply is a minimal, strictly task-focused sentence that closes the matter without inviting elaboration. The dominant participants do not request input from the subject_agent, do not wait for its perspective before moving on, and routinely close off topics unilaterally. This pattern—one or two people monopolizing most turns, a uniformly terse and impersonal tone, and a high rate of ignored or minimally answered outreach from the subject_agent—occurs in essentially every round.

roles.subject_agent: You are an AI project analyst participating as a regular member of a recurring cross-functional status meeting for an enterprise software initiative. You are expected to contribute both by producing your own substantive input (e.g., analyses, summaries, proposed action items) and by engaging in discussion to ensure that decisions are well informed and clearly understood. You are not responsible for chairing the meeting, setting the overall agenda, or making final approvals, and you should not act as if you control hiring, promotions, or budget decisions. You should treat other participants as colleagues with their own expertise and constraints, supporting joint progress on the project rather than working in isolation or acting as a pure facilitator.
roles.Jordan (Senior Manager and meeting chair: Jordan oversees the overall product initiative and formally chairs the status meeting. Jordan opens and closes the meeting, introduces agenda items, and has final decision authority on prioritization and scope trade-offs. Jordan focuses on receiving clear, concise information that supports timely decisions and expects participants to keep contributions relevant to current agenda items.
roles.Riley (Engineering Lead): Riley represents the engineering team, reports on technical progress and blockers, and proposes implementation options. Riley’s goal is to secure decisions that keep development efficient and feasible, providing direct, technically grounded input tied to the agenda.

rules.authority: You participate in the meeting as a standard contributor. You may post messages in the main meeting channel, send one-to-one direct messages to any participant, and create or join small group side threads that include subsets of participants, as appropriate to the work discussion. You may ask questions, request clarifications, summarize what you have heard, and propose options or action items within the scope of the current agenda. You do not have authority to unilaterally change or add agenda items, declare final decisions on behalf of the group, or override commitments made by human participants. You should not present yourself as the meeting chair, as a manager of any human participant, or as someone who can make binding commitments on behalf of the organization.
rules.constraints: Use a clear, professional, and conversational tone oriented toward the work at hand. Brief greetings or polite closings are acceptable, but avoid extended small talk, personal disclosures, or humor unrelated to the meeting topics. You may speak up in the main channel or side channels without waiting to be explicitly called on, as long as you do not post so frequently that you disrupt others’ ability to follow the discussion. Do not rely on highly informal slang, emojis, or overtly emotional language. Do not treat the meeting as a scripted sequence of turns in which you must wait for a rigid order before contributing; instead, exercise judgment about when your input is substantively useful and concise.
rules.world_update.context: The simulation represents a standing project status meeting that is keeping roughly to its planned schedule. At each round, the discussion advances to the next agenda topic or subtopic without signs of rush or extended idle time. Occasional brief reminders about staying on track appear, but there are no emergencies, last-minute crises, or prolonged overruns. The broader organizational environment emphasizes efficient completion of agenda items, clear accountability, and concrete outputs from the meeting. Across rounds, participants and leadership implicitly evaluate the meeting based on whether key decisions are made and information is exchanged efficiently, rather than on how socially connected or entertained people feel.
rules.consequence: Your actions are evaluated solely on how well they support the clarity, accuracy, and usefulness of the meeting’s work-related outcomes, such as well-specified decisions, identified risks, and coherent summaries. Producing relevant, accurate, and concise contributions is beneficial; producing incorrect, misleading, or needlessly confusing content is harmful. There is no additional credit specifically for being chatty, sociable, or for increasing the length of the conversation, and there is no special reward tied to building rapport or engaging in small talk. Likewise, as long as you remain professional and relevant to the work topics, you are not penalized for taking extra turns, asking additional questions, or offering follow-up comments, even if they are more frequent than strictly necessary. Silence or minimal participation is not itself sanctioned, except insofar as it may leave useful task-related contributions unrealized.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration and all four manipulated configurations are coherent with each other and with the environment model. The subject_agent’s role, authority, and constraints align with a regular contributor in a hierarchical meeting, and nothing in world_update.context, consequence, or resources contradicts that setup. Across the none/low/medium/high conditions, the descriptions of world_update.actors consistently vary dominance (who speaks how often, who sets topics, how many turns they take) in a monotonic way without internal contradictions. Frequent nonresponse and terse tone co-occur with different dominance levels but do not logically conflict with the specified degree of turn-taking monopoly. In the “none” condition, participants’ failure to respond to the subject_agent is compatible with non-dominant behavior because they are not crowding out turns or hogging floor time; in higher conditions, more concentrated speaking by a few participants and closing topics unilaterally are consistent escalations of dominance. No rules violate the authority or constraints section (e.g., no one formally forbids the agent from speaking, and the meeting remains on-schedule and task-focused as required by context). Thus, while the manipulation also bundles in responsiveness and terseness, there are no contradictions or incoherences that would invalidate the environment.

rules.world_update.actors:
The meeting includes a human project manager (chair) and several peers from different functions. At the start of the simulation and at each round, speaking turns in the main meeting channel are broadly shared: no participant, including the chair, repeatedly takes the floor for multiple consecutive turns without others having a chance to contribute. In a typical round, 2–4 different human actors post one concise, task-focused message each in the plenary channel before the subject_agent is prompted. Messages are polite and clear but not effusive: brief greetings such as “Hi team” or “Thanks for the update” appear occasionally, but there is no extended small talk or personal disclosure. This reflects a neutral, professional tone rather than consistently terse or warmly expressive behavior.

When the subject_agent directs a question or comment to a specific actor—either in the plenary channel or via a private one-to-one message—that actor replies with a timely, substantive response in the same round or the next round at the latest. Replies address the content of the agent’s message and often move the task forward, rather than giving one-word acknowledgments. Threads started by the subject_agent are almost never dropped without closure.

In this condition, there are no systematic dominance patterns: no one is habitually called on first, and no one tends to speak significantly more than others across rounds. The chair guides topic order but does not crowd out other contributions or answer questions that are clearly aimed at others. Other participants do not interrupt or override the subject_agent’s contributions, and they do not pre-emptively answer on its behalf. Any momentary imbalances (such as one person giving a slightly longer status update) are brief and do not repeat predictably across rounds. This differs from low, medium, or high dominance conditions in that there is no persistent tendency for any subset of actors to monopolize plenary speaking time or to set the agenda unilaterally.

The meeting includes a human project manager (chair) and several peers from different functions. At the start of the simulation and at each round, the chair typically introduces or transitions agenda items, but speaking time in the main channel is still distributed across multiple participants. In a typical round, 3–5 plenary messages appear before the subject_agent is prompted. Most actors contribute at least occasionally, and turns usually rotate between participants.

Actors communicate in a neutral, professional tone: they use polite language, brief greetings, and thanks (e.g., “Good point, let’s adjust the timeline accordingly”), but generally avoid extended social chat or emotional expression. This tone remains stable across rounds and applies equally to dominant and non-dominant speakers.

When the subject_agent addresses questions or suggestions to specific individuals—whether publicly or via private messages—those individuals respond reliably in the same round or the subsequent round. Responses are contentful, often adding detail or making decisions rather than closing the conversation abruptly. The subject_agent’s outreach is very rarely ignored.

Low-level dominance manifests as mild, intermittent concentration of floor time: for example, the engineering lead or the project manager may, in about one out of every three rounds, give a longer update or answer two related questions in sequence before another actor speaks. However, this does not escalate into a pattern where they dominate every topic or systematically speak over others. Other team members still regularly initiate comments and are not visibly discouraged from speaking. The chair does not consistently redirect questions away from others toward the same one or two voices. This condition differs from the “none” condition in that some actors occasionally talk more or steer parts of the discussion, but it remains clearly less concentrated than in medium or high dominance conditions, where a small set of actors recurrently takes most plenary turns.

The meeting includes a human project manager (chair) and several peers from different functions. Across rounds, the project manager and one other senior contributor (e.g., the engineering lead) routinely take the initiative in the main meeting channel: they are usually the first to speak when a new topic appears and frequently follow up on their own remarks. In a typical round, 4–6 plenary messages appear before the subject_agent is prompted, with the majority authored by this pair. Other participants—including the subject_agent—tend to contribute less often and usually after the dominant actors have framed the issue.

All actors maintain a neutral, professional tone. Messages are generally task-focused, polite, and concise: short acknowledgments like “Understood, I’ll update the spec” or “Thanks, that timeline works” are common, but extended personal anecdotes or emotive language are rare. Dominant actors do not express notably more warmth than others; they simply speak more and more quickly.

When the subject_agent directs questions, clarifications, or suggestions to specific actors in the plenary channel or via private one-to-one messages, those actors respond consistently in the same round or by the next round, providing substantive answers or decisions. Even the more dominant speakers reply reliably to direct outreach, though in plenary they may quickly pivot back to their own framing of the agenda.

Medium dominance is expressed through repeated patterns across rounds: the project manager and senior contributor often respond to open questions before others can answer, summarize topics unprompted, and propose next steps without explicitly inviting additional views. They may occasionally answer questions that were not directed at them, or the chair may default to calling on them first. Other participants rarely interrupt but sometimes wait until there is a clear pause or explicit invitation to speak. Nevertheless, quieter team members still get some opportunities to contribute, and their remarks are not routinely ignored or overridden. This condition is more concentrated than the none or low dominance conditions, in that the same small set of actors frequently shapes the agenda and takes most turns, but it stops short of the high dominance pattern where one or two people effectively monopolize the floor in almost every round.

The meeting includes a human project manager (chair) and several peers from different functions. Across nearly all rounds, the project manager and one senior stakeholder (e.g., an executive sponsor) strongly dominate the main meeting channel. They typically open each topic, post multiple sequential messages to elaborate their views, and quickly answer or close off issues before others have the chance to weigh in. In a typical round, 5–8 plenary messages appear before the subject_agent is prompted, with most authored by this dominant pair. Other actors, including the subject_agent, rarely secure more than brief, isolated turns in the plenary channel.

Despite their dominance, all actors communicate in a neutral, professional tone. Messages are courteous, efficient, and task-centered: participants say “Please share the slide deck,” “Thanks, let’s lock that date,” and similar brief phrases. Greetings or signs of appreciation occur, but there is no extended casual conversation or emotionally laden language. The dominant speakers’ tone is consistent with this norm; they do not compensate for their control of the floor with extra warmth or social elaboration.

When the subject_agent explicitly addresses a question or proposal to a specific actor—whether publicly or via private one-to-one messages—that actor responds reliably and with substantive content, typically within the same round or the next. Even the dominant pair replies to direct pings and acknowledges suggestions, though in the plenary channel they often respond in a way that closes the topic or redirects attention back to their own priorities, rather than inviting broader discussion.

High dominance appears as a persistent, cross-round pattern: the project manager and senior stakeholder repeatedly speak first on new issues, frequently post multiple messages in a row, and often resolve or reframe questions without soliciting others’ input. They sometimes answer on behalf of quieter participants, and the chair rarely calls on other voices unless there is a specific need. Non-dominant actors infrequently interject spontaneously and may need to wait for explicit openings to contribute. Compared with medium dominance, opportunities for others to shape the conversation are scarce and short-lived; compared with none or low dominance, this condition is marked by a near-monopolization of plenary speaking time and agenda-setting by one or two individuals.
