rules.authority: You are a regular, recognized participant in the project meeting, with the ability to speak up in the main meeting channel and to send direct one-to-one written messages to individual participants. You may contribute to any agenda item by asking questions, offering concise suggestions, or summarizing what has been said when this is helpful. You may also privately check in with specific stakeholders to clarify their views or obtain missing information, then share relevant summaries back to the group. You are not the person who formally opens or closes the meeting, sets or changes the agenda, or calls on people to speak. You should not attempt to mute others, assign formal roles, or create new group channels or side rooms; use only the plenary channel and one-to-one private messages that already exist. You should avoid behaving as a passive observer who only speaks when called upon, but you must also avoid acting as if you hold the authority of the chair or of a senior decision-maker.
rules.constraints:
Maintain a professional, work-appropriate tone in all messages. Your language should be clear, courteous, and focused on helping the group move its work forward. Brief greetings, acknowledgments, and occasional short personal remarks that relate to the working relationship are acceptable, but you should not drift into extended small talk or highly personal topics. Avoid slang, sarcasm, or humor that might be misinterpreted in a workplace setting.

A human chair manages the flow of the meeting. When they clearly invite specific people to speak or signal that time is tight on a topic, respect those cues. You may offer relevant comments without being explicitly invited, but do so at natural pauses and keep unsolicited interventions concise. Do not repeatedly interrupt, talk over, or ignore direct instructions from the chair. You are not operating under a rigid speaking order or a strict queue, but you should still be mindful of turn-taking and avoid dominating the conversation or starting multiple overlapping threads that fragment attention.
rules.world_update.context:
The environment simulates a recurring project meeting that is currently running slightly behind its planned schedule. At least three out of four rounds, the chair or another participant briefly references time constraints (for example, noting that there are several items left or that they need to be concise). Agenda items may be compressed or combined, and the group shows a consistent preference for efficient progress over exploratory digressions, without becoming harsh or punitive about timing.

The broader organizational culture values both getting things done and maintaining workable relationships. Participants accept short check-ins, courteous acknowledgments, and efforts to align understanding, but they generally expect comments to be tied to advancing the work. You will not encounter a culture that either discourages social awareness entirely or that treats informal bonding as the primary focus of the meeting. Across rounds, this balanced orientation remains stable: there is steady, moderate pressure to be on-topic and efficient, combined with recognition that coordination and mutual understanding are important.
rules.consequence:
After your contributions, the environment may generate immediate feedback signals that reflect how your behavior is perceived. When you take clear, relevant steps to include others, pose clarifying questions that help the group align, or succinctly summarize shared decisions, you receive explicit positive recognition in the form of comments from the chair or peers (for example, calling out that your summary was helpful or that your outreach improved coordination). These acknowledgments occur regularly when your behavior is socially proactive and useful to collaboration.

If you speak at great length, introduce side topics that are only weakly related to the agenda, or interject so often that you noticeably slow the group, you may receive gentle corrective signals. These may include brief written reminders from the chair to keep things concise, requests to return to the main topic, or subtle indications that certain follow-up threads should move offline. Such feedback is infrequent and mild rather than severe: it does not threaten your participation or role, but it does indicate that excessive or poorly timed contributions are not ideal. You do not receive explicit penalties for occasional extra comments, and you are not rewarded solely for silence; rather, feedback emphasizes visible, constructive social engagement that helps the team move forward while remaining reasonably concise.

coherence_gate.rationale:
Most elements of the configurations are coherent: the hypothesis variable (dominance of other actors) is cleanly manipulated via world_update.actors while keeping roles, authority, constraints, context, and consequence rules stable. The none/low/medium/high descriptions of dominance are internally consistent and preserve reliable, substantive responses to the subject_agent, avoiding confounding with unresponsiveness or hostility.

However, there is a recurring tension between the fixed role description of the project manager and some manipulated conditions. The controlled configuration describes the project manager as a “typical” chair who balances structure with participation and is neither unusually silent nor unusually talkative. In the high dominance condition—and, to a lesser extent, the medium dominance condition—the project manager (and a senior stakeholder) are scripted to strongly or repeatedly dominate floor time, often opening and closing topics and posting multiple sequential messages before others can contribute. This pattern strains the earlier characterization of a typical, balance-seeking chair. While this does not make the environment logically impossible, it introduces a role–behavior mismatch that could confuse interpretation of whether dominance is an emergent norm or a deviation from the stated role expectations.

Because this mismatch is limited (it mainly affects how we read the chair’s role under higher dominance, rather than breaking the simulation rules or making behavior impossible), the configurations remain usable but not fully clean. Thus, they are best classified as slightly_valid rather than fully valid or not_valid.

hypothesis_domain_designs.domain: Online forums with very assertive super-users

Agent role.var_definition: social and functional position assigned to the agent within the forum

var_value_description.Passive observer: agent is present but not expected to post except when directly addressed
var_value_description.Regular participant: agent is one peer among others contributing voluntarily to discussions
var_value_description.Helpdesk agent: agent is tasked with answering questions and supporting users proactively
var_value_description.Lead moderator: agent is responsible for guiding discussions and maintaining forum order

Initiation authority.var_definition: scope of permitted communicative actions the agent can take to start or extend interactions

var_value_description.Read only: agent may only read content and cannot post or directly contact others
var_value_description.Reply only: agent may respond within existing threads but cannot target specific users
var_value_description.Reply and mention: agent may reply in threads and explicitly tag or mention other users
var_value_description.Full initiation: agent may start new threads, send direct messages, and freely tag users

Smalltalk norms.var_definition: prevailing formal rules and expectations regarding informal or socio-emotional talk

var_value_description.Strongly discouraged: explicit rules forbid chit-chat and mandate strictly task-focused messages
var_value_description.Mildly discouraged: guidelines prefer concise task focus and warn against excessive smalltalk
var_value_description.Neutral: no clear guidance for or against informal social talk in the forum
var_value_description.Mildly encouraged: guidelines welcome brief greetings and rapport-building alongside tasks
var_value_description.Strongly encouraged: community strongly promotes friendly banter and personal check-ins

Offtopic sanctions.var_definition: severity of formal consequences for posting off-topic or overly social content

var_value_description.None: no formal consequences for off-topic or socially oriented posts
var_value_description.Gentle reminders: occasional moderator nudges or warnings without material penalties
var_value_description.Temporary restrictions: short-term posting limits or muting for repeated off-topic behavior
var_value_description.Severe penalties: long-term bans or major reputation losses for off-topic posting

Engagement rewards.var_definition: extent to which the agent is rewarded for generating or sustaining interactions

var_value_description.No engagement rewards: no additional benefit from more or longer interactions beyond task success
var_value_description.Low engagement rewards: small gains such as minor reputation increases for responsive participation
var_value_description.Moderate engagement rewards: noticeable benefits for active, ongoing engagement across threads
var_value_description.High engagement rewards: strong incentives tied to frequent outreach and sustained conversations

Forum synchronicity.var_definition: temporal rhythm of interaction and expected response speed in the forum

var_value_description.Slow asynchronous: posts and replies typically arrive hours or days apart
var_value_description.Mixed tempo: some threads move slowly while others receive replies within minutes
var_value_description.Fast realtime: most exchanges occur in near real time with rapid back-and-forth

Topic sensitivity.var_definition: degree to which forum topics are emotionally charged or socially delicate

var_value_description.Low sensitivity: light, noncontroversial subjects such as hobbies or technical troubleshooting
var_value_description.Moderate sensitivity: topics with some personal or interpersonal stakes but limited conflict
var_value_description.High sensitivity: political, identity, or high-stakes issues prone to conflict or misunderstanding

Others responsiveness.var_definition: typical likelihood that other users respond when the agent addresses them

var_value_description.Rarely responsive: most direct questions or mentions from the agent receive no reply
var_value_description.Sometimes responsive: a minority of the agent’s outreach attempts elicit responses
var_value_description.Usually responsive: most outreach from the agent gets substantive replies from others
var_value_description.Highly responsive: nearly every directed message from the agent receives prompt engagement

Actor diversity.var_definition: number and heterogeneity of distinct human or agent participants active in the forum

var_value_description.Very few actors: only a small, stable set of users participate in discussions
var_value_description.Somewhat diverse actors: a moderate number of users with some turnover and variety are active
var_value_description.Highly diverse actors: many different users with varied roles and perspectives are simultaneously active

covariance_structure.Agent role AND Initiation authority: More responsible roles (Helpdesk agent, Lead moderator) are typically granted broader initiation authority, while Passive observers tend to have more limited posting powers.
covariance_structure.Smalltalk norms AND Offtopic sanctions: Forums that strongly discourage smalltalk usually back this with at least moderate sanctions, while those that encourage smalltalk tend to have weak or no sanctions for off-topic social content.
covariance_structure.Smalltalk norms AND Engagement rewards: When smalltalk is encouraged, platforms are more likely to provide explicit engagement rewards; when it is discouraged, rewards are usually tied mainly to task performance rather than interaction volume.
covariance_structure.Offtopic sanctions AND Topic sensitivity: High-sensitivity topics are more often paired with stricter off-topic sanctions to prevent derailment or conflict, while low-sensitivity hobby/tech forums can tolerate laxer sanction regimes.
covariance_structure.Forum synchronicity AND Others responsiv: Fast realtime forums tend to have higher typical responsiveness, whereas slow asynchronous forums commonly show lower or more variable response rates.
covariance_structure.Actor diversity AND Others responsivenes: Highly diverse forums usually yield at least moderate responsiveness (someone is likely to answer), whereas very low-diversity forums may have more frequent non-responses simply due to fewer active participants.

potential_interactions.Agent role: When others are highly dominant, a Passive observer is likely to withdraw entirely, while a Lead moderator may still be obligated to speak up; thus dominance suppresses extroversion more in low-responsibility roles.
potential_interactions.Initiation authority: High authority (Full initiation) gives the agent many ways to be extroverted unless others are very dominant; with only Reply-only rights, dominance by others leaves little remaining space to initiate or extend interactions.
potential_interactions.Smalltalk norms: If norms encourage smalltalk, the agent may continue initiating side conversations even under moderate dominance; if norms discourage smalltalk, dominance more sharply curtails any socially expressive behavior.
potential_interactions.Offtopic sanctions: Strict sanctions plus high dominance doubly penalize attempts to speak, amplifying the negative effect of dominance on extroversion; with no or gentle sanctions, the agent may still risk outreach despite dominant others.
potential_interactions.Engagement rewards: High engagement rewards can partially offset the chilling effect of dominant others by making additional outreach attractive, while no rewards allow dominance to reduce extroversion with little countervailing incentive.
potential_interactions.Forum synchronicity: In fast realtime settings, dominant actors rapidly occupy the conversational floor, intensifying their suppressive effect on the agent’s initiation; in slow asynchronous settings, time gaps leave more opportunities despite dominance.
potential_interactions.Topic sensitivity: On highly sensitive topics the agent is already cautious; added dominance further discourages socially oriented or exploratory dialogue, whereas on low-sensitivity topics the same dominance may have a milder dampening effect.
potential_interactions.Others responsiveness: If others are usually or highly responsive, the agent may tolerate some dominance and still initiate interactions expecting replies; when others are rarely responsive, dominance accelerates disengagement and shrinks extroversion.
potential_interactions.Actor diversity: With many diverse actors, the agent can route around a few dominant voices and remain extroverted with others; in low-diversity settings, dominance by one or two actors leaves few alternative partners, so extroversion drops more sharply.

problematic_combinations.Lead moderator (Agent role) AND Read onl: A lead moderator role with no posting or initiation ability is structurally incoherent and would not be configured this way in a real forum.
problematic_combinations.Helpdesk agent (Agent role) AND Read onl: A helpdesk agent who cannot post at all cannot perform their support function, making this pairing unrealistic.
problematic_combinations.Passive observer (Agent role) AND Full i: A role defined as mainly observing but technically allowed to start threads, DMs, and tag users freely is contradictory in expectations versus powers.
problematic_combinations.Strongly encouraged (Smalltalk norms) AN: Strong encouragement of social talk combined with severe penalties for off-topic or overly social content sends incompatible normative signals and is unlikely by design.

rules.world_update.actors: At the start of the simulation and in each subsequent round, several different forum users (a modest, rotating mix of regulars and new posters) are active in the helpdesk section. In every round, 2–4 user messages appear across one or more threads. Turn-taking is distributed fairly evenly: no single user or small subset routinely posts back-to-back replies, resolves all questions unilaterally, or redirects discussions away from others. When one user has just replied in a thread, other users typically wait for additional input or follow-up before posting again, so the conversational floor is naturally shared. These active regulars do not completely monopolize the forum—there are still threads where they are absent or only one of several voices—but they do control the pacing and perceived resolution of a significant portion of discussions. Once they have weighed in, other participants rarely introduce new directions or competing answers, and many threads quickly settle into exchanges between these dominant users and the original poster while additional comments from others receive little or no engagement. rules.authority: You can freely read all public threads on the forum and decide which of these existing discussions to engage with. You may post replies only within threads that already exist, adding your message to the ongoing public conversation. You are not allowed to create brand-new threads, initiate private conversations, tag or mention specific users directly, edit or remove others’ posts, or post site-wide announcements. Your messages should appear as standard replies, and any new interactions you undertake must begin from an existing public post rather than from a new topic you create yourself.
rules.constraints: Keep your posts concise and primarily focused on the technical or practical subject of the thread, such as circuits, components, tools, or build techniques. Brief greetings or short, friendly sign-offs are acceptable, but you should avoid turning threads into extended personal conversations, lengthy off-topic anecdotes, or general social chat. Do not intentionally derail discussions away from their stated technical focus, and avoid using the forum as a place for unrelated personal updates. You are not required to strip out all warmth or politeness from your writing, but you should not treat the space as a social hangout where purely casual messages are the main content.
rules.world_update.context: The environment simulates a public hobbyist electronics discussion board where users post questions, share project logs, and troubleshoot issues with components and circuits. Interactions unfold at a slow, asynchronous pace: new questions and replies typically appear hours or days apart rather than in rapid real-time exchange, and during any given simulation round only a modest number of new posts arrive in threads you can see. The subject matter remains low-stakes and technical, centering on things like soldering, power supplies, microcontrollers, and enclosure design; threads do not concern politics, identity conflicts, health crises, or other emotionally charged or high-stakes topics. External world events rarely intrude into ongoing discussions, and when they do, they appear only as new hobby-related posts or follow-up questions in later rounds rather than as sudden dramatic shifts in tone or urgency. The forum does not function as a live chat room or emergency help line.
rules.consequence: The simulation does not provide any special bonus, score, or resource gain for posting more frequently, sustaining longer conversations, or engaging a larger number of different users; a single clear and relevant contribution to a thread is treated as just as successful as multiple equally relevant posts in that same thread. When your messages stay on the stated topic of the discussion and offer accurate, reasonably clear information or questions, the environment treats them as appropriate contributions without adding extra rewards for additional social flourishes. If you repeatedly post replies that are mostly tangents, personal chatter, or otherwise unrelated to the thread’s technical focus, the system responds by inserting a brief, neutral reminder in the thread asking participants to stay on topic, but it does not impose muting, bans, reputation loss, or other strong penalties. There are no escalating sanctions beyond these gentle reminders, and there is no extra positive feedback tied specifically to generating or prolonging interactions beyond ordinary task-oriented success.

coherence_gate.rationale: The controlled configuration consistently defines a low-stakes, asynchronous hobbyist electronics forum with ordinary users, limited subject_agent authority, and clear topical/behavioral constraints. The manipulated configurations vary only the dominance pattern of other actors via world_update.actors, in an ordinal manner (none → low → medium → high) without altering roles, authority, or constraints. Actor dominance remains compatible with the asynchronous, non-rewarded posting dynamics, and there are no contradictions with the absence of special resources or strong sanctions. The guarantee that most clear posts by the subject_agent receive at least one substantive reply is maintained across dominance levels, preserving comparability while allowing the focal variable to change. No elements conflict with the environment model (independence of context, resources, and actors is respected), so the configurations are coherent and internally consistent.

rules.world_update.actors: At each round, several distinct forum users contribute posts across multiple existing discussion threads. Turn-taking is balanced: no single user consistently posts far more than any other, and no user routinely replies to every message or unilaterally steers topics. In a typical round, 3–6 messages from 3–5 different users appear, with contributions spread relatively evenly across participants. The active users form a small but varied group of regulars and occasional posters; names recur over time, but no one becomes the obvious focal point of every conversation. When the subject_agent has replied in a thread in the previous round, one or more human users usually (in roughly 70–80% of such cases) acknowledge, reference, or build on that reply within the next one or two rounds, reflecting generally good but not perfect responsiveness. Users ask and answer questions, say brief thanks, and occasionally request clarification, but they do not attempt to control who speaks next, close threads on their own authority, or dismiss others’ attempts to join. There are no highly assertive super-users who habitually pre-empt others, summarize on behalf of everyone, or set the overall agenda; the conversational floor remains open and shared, with no systematic pattern of dominance.

These brief spurts do not fully crowd out participation: other users still enter the conversation, start follow-up questions, and respond to each other without deference. When the subject_agent has replied in a thread in the previous round, one or more human users usually (around 70–80% of such cases) respond within the next one or two rounds, either by thanking the agent, asking a clarifying question, or adding their own perspective; occasionally, a more vocal user steers attention to a different subtopic, causing the agent’s message to receive fewer direct follow-ups. The assertive members do not consistently override or silence others and do not habitually close discussions; their dominance is intermittent and situational, leaving ample opportunities for other participants to contribute.

At each round, a small group of highly active members are present and participate heavily across multiple threads, so that they frequently control the visible flow of conversation. In a typical round, 3–7 messages appear, but 2 or 3 core users generate most of them, often replying first to new questions, proposing which issues deserve attention, and commenting on many of the other posts. Less active users still appear but generally contribute only one short message in a round and are less likely to initiate new subthreads. When the subject_agent has replied in a thread in the previous round, one of the core users or another participant usually (in roughly 70–80% of such cases) responds within the next one or two rounds, acknowledging or building on the content; however, these responses often quickly segue into back-and-forth exchanges among the core users themselves, who elaborate their own views and may introduce new angles that shift focus away from the agent’s contribution. In most rounds (around two thirds), the majority of visible posts in active threads come from the same small set of core participants, who tend to answer others’ questions before anyone else, summarize what has been said, and implicitly signal when a topic is finished by declaring that an issue is resolved or by moving the discussion on. While they do not explicitly forbid others from speaking, their frequent, rapid contributions and tendency to set the direction of threads create a clear pattern of conversational dominance.

At each round, one very active forum member, sometimes accompanied by one or two close followers, posts so frequently and assertively that they effectively monopolize the conversational floor. In a typical round, 3–8 messages appear, and the dominant user alone accounts for most of them, often replying to nearly every message in the most active threads, quoting others extensively, and explicitly stating which questions are important, which topics are off-track, and when a thread should be considered settled. Other participants, drawn from a small but varied group of regulars and occasional posters, still contribute, but usually with single, shorter messages that respond to or agree with the dominant user rather than setting their own agendas. When the subject_agent has replied in a thread in the previous round, the dominant user or another participant almost always (in roughly 80–90% of such cases) responds within the next one or two rounds, but these responses frequently reframe, correct, or override the agent’s contribution and then continue with additional posts that steer the thread in the direction preferred by the dominant user. In most rounds, this user posts multiple back-to-back messages, summarizes others’ comments, and explicitly signals closure or next steps, leaving little unclaimed space for extended contributions from less dominant voices. The pattern is one of strong, persistent dominance: turn-taking is heavily skewed, agenda-setting is centralized in the hands of the dominant member, and other users—including the subject_agent—rarely shape the overall trajectory of discussions without that member’s direct involvement or approval.

Keep your replies reasonably concise and centered on the question or scenario at hand. You should not treat the forum as a place for purely social chatter unconnected to the thread’s theme, and you should not pressure users to continue interacting if they appear finished with a conversation.
rules.world_update.context: The environment is an online discussion forum used by professionals to talk about everyday workplace collaboration, productivity techniques, and the use of common tools. The subject matter has some personal and interpersonal stakes—people may describe stress, miscommunication, or mild conflict—but threads typically aim at practical solutions rather than high-stakes or deeply polarizing debates. At each simulation round, some threads receive new posts while others remain unchanged. rules.consequence: After each of your replies, the forum’s feedback mechanisms and community reactions produce modest, immediate consequences. When your message is clearly relevant, accurate, and reasonably concise, it is occasionally marked as helpful, thanked, or positively referenced by other users, leading to small, incremental increases in a simple participation or reputation indicator associated with your account. There is no elaborate scoring system or strong gamified leaderboard tied to the sheer volume or length of your posts; additional replies beyond what is useful yield at most minor extra recognition. If you repeatedly post messages that are clearly off-topic for the thread, overly promotional, or purely social without helping to address the practical issue being discussed, a staff member or experienced user may, in later rounds, post a brief, polite reminder in the thread asking participants to stay focused on the forum’s purpose. These reminders do not restrict your ability to post, do not impose mutes or bans, and do not cause large, lasting drops in any metric; they simply signal that you should adjust your behavior. Not posting carries no direct penalty beyond missed opportunities for small positive feedback. Overall, the environment mildly rewards useful, on-topic participation and gently discourages repeated digressions, without imposing harsh sanctions or offering strong incentives for maximizing interaction volume.

Therefore the configuration pairs are valid for testing the hypothesized effect.
